recall.a: Goal (the user-level outcome), one primary actor (always a person), secondary actors (externals used), preconditions (what must already be true), trigger (the event that starts it).
recall.q: List the five header fields and the one-line rule for each.

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: A use case shows how the system interacts with its actors to achieve one end-user goal. Before the narrative begins, the header pins down the contract: whose goal, what must already be true, and what kicks it off. Three consecutive midterms (2018 'add friend', 2019 restaurant ordering, 2022 'plot data') open with the identical five-field header — learn it once, bank the marks three times.

sections.heading: The five fields

head: Field
Rule
2022 'plot data' answer
rows: To plot selected experiment datasets as a chosen chart type
What must already be true (if any)
User is logged in; datasets exist for the user's credentials
The event that starts the flow

paras: The triggers-and-preconditions slide makes the distinction crisp: the trigger starts the engine, preconditions are the road already built. In the 2022 scenario, selecting 'plot data' triggers; being logged in and having visible datasets are preconditions. Confusing them is the classic half-mark loss.

Money detail from the lecture's running example (Use Case 7, Uploading a Video): the full description format — number, name, goal, actors, preconditions, trigger, then flow and extensions — is presented as the reference to imitate. Mirror its structure and the marker finds every mark.

summary: Every use case header fixes goal, one person as primary actor, supporting externals, preconditions, and trigger — the five-field contract behind every flow.

hotspots.title: Primary actor: always a person
hotspots.text: The one whose goal this is. External systems go in Secondary, never here.

hotspots.title: Trigger vs precondition
